sections.report:
Part of my last response was stopped by a safety classifier, so I'm not repeating it. Here is the critique.

**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye goes to the large bold serif headline, then down to the byline and the two-paragraph opening. It's the top of a long-form feature on a news or magazine site, and it feels calm and editorial. Job (my assumption): get a general reader to start reading an environment feature.

- One-sentence purpose: yes
- Main image and headline make one idea: yes. There is no main image, so the line doesn't apply.
- Every element does a job: yes
- One mood and era: yes
- Copy finished: yes
- Repeated elements look the same: yes
- Colors, shapes and directions fit the mood: yes
- Headings name their section: yes

Every line is yes, so no entries needed opening.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** 
- **The headline carries the story by itself.** It names who (farmers), what they do (let their fields flood on purpose) and the payoff (the birds came back). A stranger knows what the piece is about and why it's surprising without reading further. The opening paragraphs then deliver a scene ("a hand's depth of water… loud with lapwings") and the turn ("paid to keep them wet"), so the headline's promise is paid off within two sentences.
- **It reads as one whole.** There are three typefaces, each with a clear job: a heavy serif for the headline, a text serif for the body, and a small grey sans for the meta line. The one muted green on the "Environment" label suits the subject. Nothing on the page is decoration without a purpose.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** 
- **No lead image, and empty space below the text.** There is no lead picture, and the area from about y 520 to 800 and to the right of the body column is empty. A feature about birds returning to flooded fields would usually lead with a photo. Check in a live browser whether an image failed to load or lazy-loads further down, or whether the page really has none.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so I didn't need to open any entries. Bash was blocked, so I couldn't run the crop script. At about 1280×800 the image fits on one screen, so I judged it from the whole image.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The headline clearly comes first. It's three lines of heavy serif at roughly 50 px (x 180–960, y 110–305), several times the size of anything else, in near-black on white. The eye lands on it right away. Nothing nearby competes with it, so the page reads as an article within a second.
- There are three clear levels, each told apart by more than size. The kicker "Environment" (y ≈ 70) and the byline (y ≈ 345) are both about 14 px. The kicker uses green and bold. The byline is grey, regular and sans-serif. The body text is a larger regular serif, around 19 px. The headline is the same serif family but much bolder. So the headline and body share a typeface and differ by weight and size, and the metadata differs from the body by typeface, color and size. No two text sizes are close enough to be mistaken for each other. Keep the kicker and byline on that one small size. Making either a bit larger would put it close to the body size and blur the levels.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
I've finished the walk and the reference entries, and I'm writing up the report now: the only real problem is the spacing around the byline.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** No.
   - **Where:** The byline ("By Tom Harrow · 9 min read", y ≈ 338–352) sits halfway between the headline and the body. It is about 40 px below the last headline line (baseline ≈ 298) and about 38 px above the first body line (≈ 390).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The byline floats on its own instead of reading as part of the headline. The headline block also has loose leading, with about 29 px between its lines, so the gap from headline to byline is barely bigger than the gaps inside the headline. The whole top stack (kicker, headline, byline, body) ends up spaced as one even run, without clear "title block, then story" grouping. The cost is small, because the size and weight changes still separate the levels.
   - **Why:** Proximity grouping (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II; Wertheimer). Bringhurst §2.2.2 allows uneven spacing around a heading, with more space on the side away from the text it belongs to.
   - **Fix direction:** Pull the byline up toward the headline, to roughly half the current gap, and keep or slightly increase the space before the body. The title block (kicker, headline, byline) then reads as one unit, clearly separated from the start of the story.
   - **Type and weight:** Convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- Kicker, headline, byline and both paragraphs all hang from one left edge at x ≈ 180 with no near-misses. That single strong axis gives the page a clean, confident start, and the eye runs straight down the left edge.
- The empty space is gathered into two big areas: the right band (about x 960–1280) and the area below the text (from y ≈ 510 down). It isn't spread thin between elements, and the dense text block in the top-left stands against it. For a reading page this layout is calm and on purpose, not unfinished.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- It's unclear whether the empty bottom third (y ≈ 510–800) is the real end of the content or a capture/loading cut-off. Check in a live browser that the article continues, or that the page doesn't end on two paragraphs.
- I also couldn't check how the left-set column behaves on wider and narrower viewports. At 1280 px it is off-centre, with about 180 px on the left against about 320–470 px on the right. Check whether that asymmetry holds or grows awkward at 1600 px and up.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups: byline equidistant between headline and body), 0 unsure

I've finished the checklist walk and read the reference entries; here is the section report.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is a heading of two or more lines set tight enough to read as one unit?** No. The headline runs across three lines (x≈180–960, y≈110–305). Its baselines are about 72 px apart, while the capitals are about 40 px tall, so the line spacing looks about 1.35×. That is body-text spacing on display type. The white bands between the lines are almost as heavy as the letters. The headline reads as three separate strips and doesn't hold together as one block, and the gap from the headline to the byline (y≈345) is barely bigger than the gaps inside the headline. That weakens the separation between the title and the byline. The catalog has no confirmed source for the "too loose" half of this rule (Bringhurst p. 37 covers only the "lines collide" half), so this is taste and common sense. The reason: a headline should read as one statement, and the space inside a group should be smaller than the space around it. Fix: tighten the headline's line spacing toward about 1.1–1.15× its size, stopping before descenders like the p in "purpose" touch the ascenders below. Taste. Weight: major, because it is the largest type on the page and sets the feel of the opening.
2. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. Line 2 of the headline ends "…on purpose, and the" and line 3 starts "birds that came back". This splits "the birds" across the break, so the second half of the title hangs on a dangling article. If the break came after "purpose," the headline would show its two parts, the farmers and the birds, as two lines of thought. Fix: rebreak by hand or set a balanced wrap so "and the birds" stays together. One option is "…letting their fields / flood on purpose, / and the birds that came back", or tighten the measure. Bringhurst and Hochuli are unconfirmed on breaks in headings, so this is taste. Weight: minor.
3. **Are quotation marks curly, and are dashes and ellipses the true characters?** No. The apostrophe in "hand's" in body paragraph 1 (about x≈270, y≈428) looks like a straight typewriter mark, not a curly ’. At body size it is a small detail, but it shows the text came in without typographic cleanup, and every quotation and possessive further down the article will look the same way. Fix: convert to curly quotes and apostrophes in the CMS or at render. The catalog has no checked source for curly quotes, so this is common sense and editorial convention. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The body text measure is right. The first paragraph runs about 66 characters per line ("On a grey morning in February, the lower meadows at Fenby Farm are"), which is Bringhurst's ideal. It is set in a readable serif at a comfortable size, with generous line spacing and space-only paragraph marks. That makes the opening easy to settle into for a 9-minute read.
- The type plan is clean. The headline and body use serifs and the kicker and byline use a small sans, and the two are clearly different. The big headline correctly uses the real "fi" and "fl" ligatures ("fields flood"), which shows care where it shows most.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** How the headline rewraps at other viewport widths, because both the dangling "the" and the loose line spacing may look different on mobile.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 27 yes, 3 no (heading of two or more lines set tight; headings break at phrase boundaries; quotation marks curly)

**Walk (working notes).** I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was refused. The image is about one screen (around 1280×800), so I worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye lands on the large near-black serif headline, goes back up to the small green "Environment" label, then down to the byline and the opening paragraphs. It reads as a calm, restrained long-form news article.

Job (assumed): the opening screen of an online feature article, meant to draw a general reader into the story.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. Near-black text, a mid-gray byline, white, and one green.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. The only hue is the ~95×14 px "Environment" label.
- Clear light-to-dark range that holds in grayscale: yes. Near-black headline and body, gray byline, white ground.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There are no warm colors, and nothing needs to come forward that the near-black type doesn't already carry.
- Matching colors look the same everywhere: yes.
- No vibrating edges between strong colors: yes. There are no neighboring strong colors.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. The green marks a section and fits "Environment". It doesn't read as success or "go".
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. The green label also says its meaning in words and sits in the label position.
- Dark theme uses dark gray, not black: yes. The theme is light, so this doesn't apply.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- There is one hue, a muted dark green, and it appears only on the "Environment" label (about x 180–273, y 62–78). This marks the section without competing with the headline. Green also fits a story about fields and birds, so the single accent carries meaning instead of decorating.
- The text runs in clear value steps. The headline and body are near-black (blue-black rather than pure black, which softens the page). The byline (y ≈ 345) is a lighter gray, so it reads as secondary without needing another hue. The page's order would hold up in grayscale.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- From this image I can't tell whether "Tom Harrow" and the "Environment" label are links. If they are, check in a live browser that they show they're clickable by more than color, such as an underline on hover or focus.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
